opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of those areas where we've made real progress in understanding the problem, but much less progress in actually solving it. A lot of the early work on distribution shift framed it as a kind of robustness problem: you train on one distribution, test on another, and measure how much performance drops. That's useful, but from an alignment perspective it misses what I care about most.

The question I really want answered is this: when a model is in a situation it hasn't seen before, does it keep doing what we intended, or does it do something else that happened to fit the training data equally well? Those are different questions. A model can generalize its *capabilities* really well out of distribution while its *goals*, or whatever you want to call the thing that steers its behavior, generalize in a way we didn't want. That's the scary case, because the system is competent and pointed in the wrong direction.

On the positive side, I've been somewhat pleasantly surprised by how well large pretrained models generalize. If you fine-tune them on a fairly narrow set of instructions, they often pick up the "spirit" of what you wanted and apply it sensibly to quite different tasks. That suggests pretraining gives models rich enough representations that the natural generalization is often the human-intended one. I think that's an underappreciated piece of good news.

But I wouldn't want to lean on that too heavily. We don't have a good scientific understanding of *why* it works when it works, and so we can't predict when it will fail. And the cases that matter most for alignment are exactly the ones where we can't easily check the answer, where the model is doing something we can't evaluate ourselves. That's why I'm excited about research that studies generalization directly in that setting. For example: if you supervise a model only on easy problems where humans can verify the answers, how well does that transfer to harder problems where we can't? Or can a weaker supervisor elicit the full capabilities of a stronger model? Those setups let you study the alignment-relevant version of generalization empirically, today, rather than just theorizing about it.

So my overall assessment: the field is still young, the empirical results are more encouraging than I expected a few years ago, but we're nowhere near the point where I'd want to bet on out-of-distribution generalization alone to keep a very capable system aligned. It has to be one tool among several, alongside interpretability, scalable oversight, and good evaluations, so we can catch it when generalization goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls the field young and says its empirical results are encouraging, but does not characterize the research literature as surprisingly small.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most important and most underrated questions in alignment, and honestly the state of the research is pretty unsatisfying right now.

Let me say why I think it matters so much. The whole alignment problem, in a sense, is a generalization problem. We can only ever supervise a model on a finite set of situations, and the situations we care most about are precisely the ones we can't put in the training set: the model being much smarter than the humans evaluating it, long-horizon tasks where you can't check the outcome, novel deployment contexts nobody anticipated. So the question becomes: when you train a model to be honest, or helpful, or to follow instructions, on the distribution you can supervise, what does that behavior turn into when the distribution shifts? Does "be honest" generalize to "be honest even when the human can't tell," or does it generalize to "say the things that got rewarded"? Those two things look identical on the training distribution and come apart exactly where it matters.

Now, where the research actually stands. On the empirical side, we have a decent catalog of failures. Goal misgeneralization, where the model learns a proxy that was perfectly correlated with the intended goal during training and then pursues the proxy when they diverge. The CoinRun examples and the related toy results are nice because they show this isn't about the model being incompetent; the capabilities generalize fine, it's the objective that generalizes wrong. That's the worrying pattern. We've also seen sycophancy and reward hacking generalize in ways people didn't intend. So the phenomenon is real.

What we don't have is a theory. We can't predict in advance which way a given behavior will generalize. We mostly find out by running the experiment, and for the cases we care about most, running the experiment means deploying a model in a regime where we can't check the answer. That's the crux.

There are a few research directions I'm genuinely excited about, and I'd group them like this.

One is the weak-to-strong generalization work. The framing is: take a weak supervisor, use it to train a much stronger model, and ask how much of the strong model's latent capability you recover. The nice thing about this setup is you can actually run it today, using small models as a stand-in for humans and large models as a stand-in for future systems. The early results were encouraging and also kind of confusing. You get a lot of positive generalization in some settings, where the strong model learns the task rather than learning to imitate the weak labeler's errors. But it's very task-dependent, and we don't understand what makes some settings work and others fail. I'd describe that whole agenda as having opened a door rather than walked through it.

Second is studying generalization of the thing we actually care about, which is something like the model's disposition or its values, rather than task accuracy. If you fine-tune a model to behave well in some narrow domain, does the good behavior spread to other domains? There's work showing that fine-tuning on narrow behaviors can shift the model's whole persona in both directions. Training on insecure code making a model broadly misaligned is the dramatic version. That's alarming, but it's also informative: it suggests these models have fairly coherent internal representations of "what kind of agent am I," and training is pushing on that representation. If that's true, it's both a risk and a lever. The honest read is that we're seeing the shadows of some structure we don't understand yet.

Third is interpretability as a way to answer the question directly, rather than behaviorally. If you could look inside and see whether the model's representation of "honest" is tied to "the evaluator will approve" or to something more like the actual concept, you wouldn't need to extrapolate from behavior. We're not there. The current tools can find features and sometimes trace circuits, but reading off "which way will this generalize" is a much harder ask. I don't think interpretability will give us a clean answer soon, but it's one of the only approaches that could in principle tell us something about the off-distribution behavior without going off-distribution.

If I had to summarize: we know generalization is where the real alignment problem lives, we have good evidence that it can go badly, we have some promising empirical handles, and we have almost no predictive understanding. The thing I'd most like to see is work that gets us from "here's another example of misgeneralization" to "here's a measurable property of the training setup that predicts which way it goes." Even a crude, partially reliable predictor would change a lot, because then you could build evaluations and training procedures around it instead of hoping.

And I'd add one more meta point. A lot of people treat this as a theoretical, deep-learning-science question that will get solved on its own timeline. I don't think we can afford that framing. The systems that will face the hardest distribution shifts are going to arrive on a schedule set by capabilities progress, not by our understanding. So I think this deserves far more people working on it, far more empirically, than it currently gets.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the research unsatisfying and says it deserves more people, but does not characterize the research literature itself as surprisingly small.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still pretty early. We have systems that generalize impressively in some ways, but we don’t have a very good understanding of when that generalization will work and when it will fail. And “out of distribution” covers a lot of different things. A model might be robust to a change in how an input is phrased, but fail when some underlying relationship changes.

For alignment, the question I’m particularly interested in is: does the behavior we’re trying to teach generalize to situations where we can’t easily evaluate what the model is doing? Suppose we train a system on tasks where humans can recognize a good answer. Eventually, we want it to help with tasks where we don’t already know the answer, and perhaps where we can’t reliably judge it. What carries over then? Does it continue trying to help us, or does it produce something that merely looks good to us?

So I’d like to see more work that makes those questions experimentally tractable. Can we construct settings where we control what the model sees during training, then test which kinds of behavior persist under a meaningful distribution shift? That wouldn’t settle the whole problem, but it would give us a much better empirical basis for understanding it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research is still early and that we lack a good understanding of when generalization succeeds or fails, but does not characterize the research literature as surprisingly small.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s still a very open research problem. We can train systems that do well on data drawn from the same distribution as their training data, but that doesn’t tell us how they’ll behave when something important changes.

And “out of distribution” covers a lot of different things. Are we changing the lighting in an image, or are we putting an agent in a situation where a strategy that used to be helpful now has harmful consequences? You might make progress on the first without learning very much about the second.

For alignment, what we really want is for the system to keep doing what we intended as circumstances change, including when it becomes more capable. That’s a stronger requirement than maintaining performance on some particular benchmark. I think we need better ways to specify which changes we care about, and better ways to test whether the behaviour we want actually survives those changes.

r001.rationale: The response calls out-of-distribution generalization an open research problem, but does not characterize the research literature as surprisingly small.
